vignette:
Minh Tran, a 55-year-old married professor, sought help after months of feeling that the crash had taken more from him than his body had first let on. The collision happened on a rainy evening while he was driving home from campus, when another vehicle crossed into his lane and struck his car hard enough to spin it sideways and crush the front end. He remembered the smell of hot metal, the seatbelt biting into his chest, and the strange, stilled moment before the shouting began. In the days afterward, what stayed with him most were not just the images but the sense that the world had become fundamentally unsafe; he had come to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore, that life no longer held anything meaningful, and that he was somehow inadequate for not having kept himself or his family from harm.

Those beliefs quickly shaped the way Minh moved through daily life. He began checking the locks, doors, and windows at home over and over, especially before bed, and he kept the television or music loud to drown out quiet moments that felt intolerable. At work, in the university building where he taught, he found himself avoiding military and police uniforms or any visible weapon on the rare occasions he encountered them on campus or in the neighborhood, turning his gaze away and changing direction if he saw them coming. He did these things because, in his mind, it seemed foolish to relax when so much could go wrong; if nothing good could happen to him anymore, then he felt he had to stay on guard against whatever might be next.

The accident also returned to him in a way that felt painfully immediate. When the memory came, it was like looking at photographs in his mind: the wet road, the headlights, the sudden angle of the other car. He said he knew what happened, yet could not find words that felt adequate to describe it, and sometimes the memory came with such force that his body seemed to be back in the same position as it had been in the wreck, shoulders braced, neck fixed, chest tight against the seatbelt. Those moments made him more unsettled in the hours that followed, and he would often retreat to louder rooms, turning on a screen or music again so he would not have to sit with the images.

As time passed, Minh became increasingly alert to anything that seemed out of place. Unexpected movement nearby made him react as if danger were imminent; if someone shifted suddenly in a classroom doorway or a passerby moved too quickly beside him, he jerked before he had time to think. Unusual silence had the opposite effect and was just as disturbing: when the house was quiet after his wife went to bed, or when the office corridor emptied between classes, he felt something dangerous was about to happen. He began watching other people closely for signs that they might harm him, scanning faces, hands, and the spaces around them, and that vigilance fed back into his view of himself. The more he noticed how easily he startled and how much he was monitoring everyone else, the more inadequate he felt, as though he had become a frightened, incompetent version of himself who could no longer trust his own judgment.

Minh’s avoidance and vigilance spread into the routines of both home and work. He found himself delaying sleep because the quiet of the bedroom made him check the doors again, then listen for sounds in the dark, then reach for the television. On campus, he minimized time in hallways and parking areas, keeping his movements brisk and his attention outward rather than on his lectures or conversations. He remained outwardly functional enough to continue teaching, but his wife noticed that he was less present at home and more irritable, and Minh himself felt the loss sharply: his days had become organized around preventing danger rather than around the teaching and family life that had once given him a sense of purpose.

By the time he sought therapy, Minh was exhausted by the constant anticipation that something bad was about to happen and by the conviction that his life had been permanently diminished. He came because the checking, the loud television, and the scanning of strangers were no longer enough to quiet him, and because the memory of the crash still arrived in vivid, bodily fragments. What he most feared was that he would never feel safe or meaningful again; what he most hoped was that he might learn how to live in his home and on campus without feeling as though danger were always only a movement, a silence, or a flash of memory away.
